title: Numbers & shopping
verifiedBy: Fable (Claude Fable 5) — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The price question is still verbless: bi-kam hādhā? is literally "for how much [is] this?" — M2's bi- ("with, in, for") doing the price job, glued to kam, and no verb anywhere in the sentence.
kam ("how many") takes a SINGULAR noun: kam kitāb ʿindaka?, never *kam kutub. English "how many books" makes the plural feel compulsory, and it is the commonest thing to get wrong here.

One is not a number placed in front of the noun. The noun comes first and wāḥid follows it like an adjective, agreeing with it: kitāb wāḥid, sayyāra wāḥida. Often the bare noun already means one, and wāḥid is added only for emphasis.

Two is not a word at all — it is a DUAL ending welded onto the noun itself: kitāb becomes kitābān, two books, with no number in sight. This is the dual's single appearance in L1: it never turns up on verbs or adjectives here.

From three onwards the number finally does stand in front, and the noun goes PLURAL: thalātha kutub, khamsa riyālāt. So Arabic counts in three different shapes depending on how many — one, two, and three-or-more.

Gender polarity, 3 to 10: the number takes the OPPOSITE marker from the noun's singular. kitāb is masculine, so the number wears -a — thalātha kutub. sayyāra is feminine, so the number goes bare — thalāth sayyārāt. Numbers are the one word class that disagrees on purpose.

"Numbers just go in front of the noun" is the slogan that hides all of the above. Learn each count with the shape it takes — kitāb wāḥid, kitābān, thalātha kutub — not as a rule about where the number sits.

min faḍlika is one expression, learned whole: "of your favour", i.e. please. Its min is not M1's "from" and cannot be pulled out of it. Like every address since M2 it is gendered — min faḍlika to a man, min faḍliki to a woman.

hādhā points at a masculine thing and hādhihi at a feminine one, and the sentence around them stays verbless: hādhā ghālī, hādhihi as-sayyāra ghāliya. It is the pointing word every shop conversation runs on.

ghālī is written the way it is said in pause. Full MSA spells this class of adjective ghālin, with an ending that carries only case — the thing this course drops everywhere — and in pause that ending is not pronounced at all: the word simply ends in a long ī.

Plurals here are vocabulary, not a system. kitāb becomes kutub by breaking apart inside; sayyāra becomes sayyārāt by adding a tail. Arabic does both, and which one a noun takes is learned with the noun.
Shopping reuses the verbs you already run. ashtarī (I buy) works exactly like M3's ashrab — a- for I, ta- for you-m or she, ya- for he — and M6's sa- puts it in tomorrow: sa-ashtarī.

sentences.cue: How many books do you have? (to a man)

words.note: "How many" — and the noun after it is singular, always: kam kitāb, kam sayyāra. English puts the plural there; Arabic never does. With bi- glued on it asks a price: bi-kam.

sentences.trap: kam kutub is the English shape and it is wrong. One kam, one singular noun — the number is what the question is asking for, so the noun does not pre-empt it.
sentences.sound: KAM ki-TAAB ʿIN-da-ka — three short beats, and the question is carried by kam alone.

variations.cue: How many cars do you have? (to a man)
variations.changed: any noun follows kam — and it stays singular

variations.cue: How many books do you have? (to a woman)
variations.changed: -aka → -aki: the question turns to a woman

variations.cue: How many books does he have?
variations.changed: -aka → -ahu: asking about him rather than asking him — the suffix is the whole pivot

mistake.why: The English plural, imported. After kam the noun is singular whatever the answer turns out to be: kam kitāb ʿindaka?

sentences.usage: Taking stock — of books, of cars, of anything countable.
sentences.mnemonic: kam takes one: the question asks for the number, so the noun stays alone.

words.note: M2's bi- ("with, for") glued to kam: "for how much?". It is the whole price question — there is no verb in it and none is missing. Two words on the page in English, one in Arabic.
"This", pointing at a masculine thing; hādhihi at a feminine one — hādhā al-kitāb, hādhihi as-sayyāra. The first ā is in the romanization but not the Arabic spelling — an old irregular spelling.

sentences.trap: No verb, and no "is": the whole question is two words. Reaching for a "costs" or a "does" is the English habit.
sentences.sound: bi-KAM HAA-dhā — the dh is the soft one, as in English "this".

variations.cue: How much is this one? (a feminine thing)
variations.changed: hādhā → hādhihi: pointing at something feminine

variations.cue: How much is this book?
variations.changed: name the thing: hādhā goes in front and the noun keeps its al-

variations.cue: How much is this car?
variations.changed: a feminine thing named: hādhihi in front, and the noun keeps its al-

mistake.why: Without bi- this asks "how many is this?", which is not a price question. The bi- is what turns the counting word into a cost: bi-kam hādhā?

sentences.usage: The first thing anyone says in a shop.
sentences.mnemonic: bi-kam — "by how much": the b buys it.

sentences.cue: I'd like some bread, please (to a man)

words.note: "Of your favour" — please. Learned as one expression: the min in it is not M1's "from" and cannot be lifted out. Gendered like every address since M2: min faḍlika to a man, min faḍliki to a woman.

sentences.trap: A request drops al-, as it has since M1: urīd khubz asks for some bread; urīd al-khubz asks for that particular loaf, the one already on the counter.
sentences.sound: u-REED KHUBZ, min FAḌ-li-ka — faḍl has the heavy ḍ in its middle.

variations.cue: I'd like a coffee, please (to a woman)
variations.changed: -ka → -ki: the request turns to a woman

variations.cue: Please, I'd like some bread
variations.changed: the courtesy can open the sentence instead of closing it

variations.display: urīd khubz wa ḥalīb, min faḍlika
variations.cue: I'd like some bread and milk, please (to a man)
variations.changed: wa joins the two things asked for — both bare, and the courtesy still closes it

mistake.why: The expression cannot be said without a person on the end of it. There is no bare "please" here: it is min faḍlika to a man and min faḍliki to a woman, and the suffix is what makes it an address at all.

sentences.usage: Buying anything at all. The courtesy is not optional in a shop.
sentences.mnemonic: min faḍlika — "from your favour": the please that asks a favour outright.

words.note: "One" — and it does not go in front. It follows its noun like an adjective and agrees: kitāb wāḥid, sayyāra wāḥida. A bare noun already means one, so wāḥid is added when the count matters.

sentences.trap: *wāḥid kitāb is the English order and no Arabic ever puts it that way. One is the only number that follows its noun.
sentences.sound: ʿIN-dee ki-TAAB WAA-ḥid — the ḥ of wāḥid is the breathy one, from the throat.

variations.cue: I have one car
variations.changed: a feminine noun, so the number takes -a like any adjective

variations.cue: I have a book
variations.changed: drop wāḥid — the bare noun already means one

variations.cue: I have only one book
variations.changed: faqaṭ closes the count: just the one — and wāḥid still follows its noun

mistake.why: English word order. One is the number that FOLLOWS its noun, agreeing with it like an adjective: kitāb wāḥid. Only three and up go in front.

sentences.usage: Correcting an assumption — no, just the one.
sentences.mnemonic: wāḥid comes after, because one is what a noun already was.

words.note: Two books, in one word: kitāb plus the dual ending -ān. No number word at all — Arabic marks two on the noun itself, and every noun can: sayyāratān. This course writes the -ān form throughout.

sentences.trap: Do not look for the word "two". It is inside the noun, and a sentence with a number word in it would be saying something else.
sentences.sound: ʿIN-dee ki-taa-BAAN — the ending is long and takes the stress.

variations.cue: I have two cars
variations.changed: the same ending on a feminine noun — and its hidden t wakes up, as in sayyāratī

variations.cue: He has two books
variations.changed: -ī → -ahu: whose books they are

variations.cue: There are two books on the table
variations.changed: the dual out in the world: hunāka announces it, and still no number word

mistake.why: The number "two" exists, but it is not how you count two things: the noun carries the dual by itself. ʿindī kitābān — one word, two books.

sentences.usage: Counting the small numbers that come up every day.
sentences.mnemonic: kitāb-ān — the ān is the pair; no number needed.

sentences.cue: I'd like three books, please (to a man)

words.note: Three — and from three onwards the number stands in front of the noun. It wears the marker opposite to the noun's gender: thalātha before masculine kitāb, bare thalāth before feminine sayyāra.
The plural of kitāb, made by breaking the word open from inside rather than adding to the end. Many nouns do this and there is no rule to derive it — kutub is learned with kitāb, as a pair.

sentences.trap: Three counts differently from two, which counts differently from one. Three shapes, not one rule about placement.
sentences.sound: u-REED tha-LAA-tha KU-tub, min FAḌ-li-ka — the th is the soft one, as in English "think".

variations.cue: I'd like five books, please (to a man)
variations.changed: any number from three to ten behaves the same way

variations.cue: I have three books
variations.changed: from asking to owning — the count does not change

variations.cue: I'd like three books, please (to a woman)
variations.changed: -ka → -ki: the same order, placed with a woman

mistake.why: kitāb is masculine, so the number takes the -a: thalātha kutub. The bare thalāth is for feminine nouns — thalāth sayyārāt. The number wears the marker its noun does not.

sentences.usage: Buying more than a couple of anything.
sentences.mnemonic: thalātha kutub, thalāth sayyārāt: the -a goes where the noun's -a is not.

words.note: The plural of sayyāra, made the other way — by adding -āt, the silent -a dropping to make room. Not every such noun takes this tail, so a plural is still learned with its noun. Two: sayyāratān (S05).

sentences.trap: sayyāra is feminine, so the number goes BARE: thalāth sayyārāt. The -a that looks feminine belongs on the number only when the noun is masculine.
sentences.sound: ʿIN-da-hu tha-LAATH say-yaa-RAAT — the plural tail takes the stress.

variations.cue: I have three cars
variations.changed: -ahu → -ī: whose cars they are

variations.cue: He has three books
variations.changed: a masculine noun, so the number puts its -a back on

variations.cue: There are three cars in front of the house
variations.changed: the counted plural announced: hunāka in front, amām says where

mistake.why: sayyāra is feminine, so its number goes bare: thalāth sayyārāt. Putting the -a on both is agreement — and numbers from three to ten are the one class that refuses to agree.

sentences.usage: Talking about what someone else owns.
sentences.mnemonic: sayyārāt — the -āt tail is the everyday plural of an -a noun.

words.note: The same bi- as bi-kam and M2's bi-khayr, now answering instead of asking: bi-khamsa, "for five". khamsa before a masculine noun, bare khams before a feminine one, exactly like thalātha.
riyāl is the currency this course prices in — one riyāl, five riyālāt, the -āt tail of sayyārāt. Masculine, so the number before it wears its -a: khamsa riyālāt. With bi-: bi-riyāl, "for a riyal".

sentences.trap: The answer to bi-kam? starts with the same bi-. Question and answer share the preposition, which is what makes the exchange feel like one sentence cut in half.
sentences.sound: HAA-dhā bi-KHAM-sa ri-yaa-LAAT — the kh is the Scottish-loch sound, as in al-khubz.

variations.cue: This one is five riyals (a feminine thing)
variations.changed: hādhā → hādhihi: pointing at something feminine

variations.cue: This is one riyal
variations.changed: one riyal, and the number goes back behind its noun

variations.cue: This book is five riyals
variations.changed: the thing named in full: hādhā al-kitāb up front, and the bi- price holds

mistake.why: Without bi- this says "this is five riyals" in the sense of being them, not costing them. A price takes the preposition: hādhā bi-khamsa riyālāt.

sentences.usage: The shopkeeper's half of the exchange.
sentences.mnemonic: bi- asks the price and bi- answers it.

sentences.cue: This one is expensive and this one is cheap

words.note: "Expensive" — ghālī of a masculine thing, ghāliya of a feminine one. Written as said when the sentence stops on it: full MSA's case ending vanishes in pause and the word ends in a long ī.
"Cheap", and the plain opposite of ghālī with none of its spelling trouble: rakhīṣ of a masculine thing, rakhīṣa of a feminine one. The ṣ at the end is the heavy s, as in aṣ-ṣabāḥ.

sentences.trap: Two verbless sentences joined by wa, and neither of them has an "is". The whole comparison is four words.
sentences.sound: HAA-dhā GHAA-lee wa HAA-dhā ra-KHEEṢ — ghālī opens with the gargled gh of ghadan.

variations.cue: This one is expensive and this one is cheap (feminine things)
variations.changed: both point at feminine things, so both adjectives take -a

variations.cue: The car is very expensive
variations.changed: name the thing, and M3's jiddan turns it up

variations.cue: Is this expensive?
variations.changed: hal + the pointing word: the shop question in three words

mistake.why: hādhā points at a masculine thing, so its adjective stays bare: hādhā ghālī. The -a belongs with hādhihi — the agreement law from M1, running inside a price.

sentences.usage: Choosing between two of the same thing, out loud, in front of the person selling them.
sentences.mnemonic: ghālī is dear and rakhīṣ is a bargain — the two words a market runs on.

sentences.cue: I buy the fruit from the market

words.note: "I buy" — the same non-past machine as M4's ashrab: a- for I, ta- for you-m or she, ya- for he. Its long final ī is part of the verb, not a trimmable ending. With M6's sa-: sa-ashtarī.

sentences.trap: This min is M1's "from", standing free and meaning exactly what it says — nothing like the min locked inside min faḍlika.
sentences.sound: ash-ta-REE al-FAA-ki-ha min as-SOOQ — the final ī is long and holds.

variations.display: ashtarī al-khubz min as-sūq kull yawm
variations.script: أشتري الخبز من السوق كل يوم
variations.cue: I buy the bread from the market every day
variations.changed: M4's kull yawm makes it a habit

variations.cue: I will buy the fruit tomorrow
variations.changed: M6's sa- moves the shopping to tomorrow

variations.cue: He buys the bread from the market
variations.changed: a- → ya-: he — the shopping verb runs the same prefix machine as ashrab

mistake.why: min faḍlika is one frozen expression meaning please, and its min cannot be borrowed to mean "from". Buying from a place takes the plain preposition: min as-sūq.

sentences.usage: Where you shop, said as a habit rather than a plan.
sentences.mnemonic: ashtarī — the shopping verb; sūq is where it happens.

comprehensionPool.cue: I'd like a coffee, please (to a woman)
How many cars does he have?

comprehensionPool.display: ashtarī al-khubz min as-sūq kull yawm
comprehensionPool.script: أشتري الخبز من السوق كل يوم
comprehensionPool.cue: I buy the bread from the market every day
The bread is cheap and the milk is expensive
There are two cars in front of the house
I buy the milk from the market
